Script:


Deon Meyer
2nd Draft Script
14 October 2019

Voice
Once in a while an author comes along with stories able to capture the imaginations of millions.

Sound Up Trackers
Milla: Whatever is happening here, it’s bigger than the both of us.

Voice
South African thriller writer Deon Meyer is one such scribe. His crime fiction novels like Dead Before Dying, Icarus and The Last Hunt have taken Meyer from local household name to internationally recognised best seller. And the adaptation of his novel Trackers, Africa’s biggest ever original television drama, is set to hit our screens next week. We met the 61 year old at the Stellenbosch home he shares with wife Marianne and their children.

Link Mac
Deon says the one thing he remembers most of his fairly modest yet happy childhood years was an absolute love of reading. A passion supported by his parents.

Sound Up Deon
I grew up in Klerksdorp, mining town, we were three boys. Lived in a sort of a lower middle class neighbourhood. And then we read. I think one of the greatest things that ever happened to me was that both my parents loved books. We couldn’t afford to buy them but Klerksdorp despite everything else had a fantastic library.

Voice
Life in Klerksdorp was a far cry from the life the globetrotting author now lives. He got his first ever new pair of shoes as a teenager, and the only travelling he did in those days was by bicycle. But crucially, it’s also when he was first introduced to the crime fiction genre.

Sound Up Deon
Deon: I remember I would go collect cold-drink bottles all over town, go trade them in for money, and then go to Don’s Book Exchange, which was quite a ride by bicycle back then. And go buy the new Ed Mcbain, the new John D Mcdonald. Not realising back then that I was laying the foundation for a career.

Voice
Some of his first attempts were short stories, written in between holding down a full-time job in advertising and raising a family.

Sound Up Deon.
I was a single parent at the time. So the only time I had to spare was between four and seven o clock in the morning when the kids were asleep.

Voice
Michele Magwood is the books editor for the Sunday Times, and has followed Meyer’s career since the very beginning.

Sound Up Michele
He just got it, straight out of the starting gate. And I think he sold his first stories to Huisgenoot. And the bug bit. And he started writing more.




Voice
His first mainstream success came with the publication of the full-length Afrikaans novel Fenix in 1996, later translated to English as Dead Before Dying. Michele says Meyer’s magical touch lies in getting readers to connect with his characters on a personal level.

Sound Up Michele Magwood
We’ve come to care for his characters. And he’s got several starring ones, and we’ll say this is a Benny Griessel book. And we come to care about them. Benny is an alcoholic, and you’ll open the book and say oh he’s drinking again. So we feel this personal relationship with his characters.

Voice
Griessel is the fan-favourite hero of several of Meyer’s books. But the author says he didn’t originally intend to have Benny, an alcoholic detective from the Hawks, play anything more than a bit part.

Sound Up Deon
Mac: Oom Deon, who’s Benny? Take us through this Benny character that feauters so much in your books?

Deon: Benny absolutely happened by chance. Benny was never supposed to be a major character. When I was writing my second novel, I needed a character to just be in one scene. He had only one task and that is to walk in on the protagonist and spoil his fun, and he had to be drunk to do that. So on the fly I created a character, a cop, an alcoholic cop. And he kept coming back. And at the end of the book I thought wow, he took up half the story. He became one of the major characters in the book.

Voice
Today Meyer has 14 novels under his belt, his books have been translated into 27 languages and published in 40 countries world-wide.

Sound Up Michele Magwood
He’s won fans all over the world. He’s particularly popular in France. I went to a book festival with him. And they love him. He gets mobbed in the street, it’s Deon! Deon! you know, and they absolutely adore him.

Voice
When not writing, Meyer is a passionate family man and Springbok supporter. To get away from it all he loves nothing more than mountain biking in the scenic Stellenbosch wilds with Marianne, who’s an avid painter.

Sound Up Marianne
At home he’s homely, he’s warm, he’s quiet. He’s quite an introvert, which I like. And he’s a lot of fun, he has a very good sense of humour, so we laugh a lot. We laugh about stupid things, but that’s the magic.

Voice
Even though the couple travel the globe together, most of the magic happens right here in South Africa.

Sound Up Deon
Mac: So do you have a favourite spot where you sit and you do your writing?

Deon: Here, right here.

Mac: Oh, ok.

Deon: What I do is I close all the blinds, and I keep it very dark. I have only one light on, no distractions. Writing is hard work, its not that sort of starry eyed thing where you stare into the distance and get inspired you know. It’s much more perspiration than it is inspiration.

Voice
Inspiration does come when he travels both locally and abroad - gaining intimate knowledge of the types of people and places he writes about.

Link Mac
He’ll often spend days on the streets of exotic locations like Bordeaux France, where he’ll meticulously plan, photograph and research scenes for upcoming novels.

Voice
Following the same routes his characters will eventually travel in his stories, Deon takes photographs like this one, of the view from beneath the organ in the Bordeaux Cathedral where a clandestine meeting takes place in the book the Last Hunt.

Sound Up Deon
This is the South African Embassy in Paris, it’s one of those either you love it or you hate it buildings, but there’s a lot going down in this building in the book as well.

Voice
Marianne often joins Deon on his travels, and loves watching the creative process unfold.

Sound Up Marianne
When you see him before the book, and the whole process going… And then the wonderful thing is afterwards, to read that book, and to see what actually happened to him. Ja, that is quite amazing.

Voice
Meyer has been hard at work collaborating with producers at home and abroad on the television adaptation of his novel Trackers, a story featuring a terrorism plot in Cape Town, a Rhino poaching syndicate and a single mother who is thrown into the clandestine world of intelligence gathering. And if this exlusive sneak peek is anything to go by, it’s going to be a scorcher.

Sound Up Trackers

Sound Up Deon
The toughest audience to please with a tv series is people who’ve read the book. Because it’s very hard to compete with the pictures they had in their minds of the characters and of the environment in which it happens.

Voice
Meyer was heavily involved in the script development for the series. He says he’s been blown away by the performances of the mainly South African cast.

Sound Up Deon`
So much so that I can’t think of the characters anymore without seeing their faces, without seeing their personalities.

Voice
Sisanda Henna plays the gangster Inkunzi the Bull. A method actor to the core, Sisanda says he spent time with real members of the underworld to get into the role.

Sound Up Siasanda
And then having frank conversations with these guys. Everything from taking a life…

Sound Up Trackers
Inkunzi: If I can talk… Then you are dead.

Sound Up Sisanda
And I found very interesting things like yes, this guy operates in a an illegal fashion, but there’s honour in it. There’s like loyalty.

Sound Up Deon
Sisanda was fantastic. I mean that scene where the hijacking of the rhino’s takes place, I mean that is just scary stuff.

Sound Up Sisanda
Mzanzi and Africa can be world class. So it starts with the writing, the thriller, how it’s plotted, how it’s tied together. And then it’s executed in the quality of the production, I mean the production quality as you say, is epic.

Voice
Meyer is already working on his next project - and it’s heartening to know that despite his international success, he says he’s staying right here to tell the stories of the people and the country he loves so much.

Sound Up Deon
Deon: I’m not going anywhere. You know people forget about all the good things in this country. People forget that at grassroots level the relationships between ordinary people are fantastic. An people must keep the faith, stay and make a difference.
